content: Rhinitis is a complex and diverse condition that is often underestimated in its significance. It is a widespread global disease that can profoundly affect the quality of life of those who suffer from it. Rhinitis is defined by the presence of one or more nasal symptoms, including sneezing, nasal itching, rhinorrhea (both anterior and posterior), and nasal congestion. The degree of nasal inflammation can vary among individuals. This condition imposes a substantial financial burden on society, with direct healthcare costs in the United States alone ranging from $1.6 to $4.9 billion annually. Additionally, the indirect costs due to lost productivity are estimated to be between $0.1 and $9.7 billion per year. Chronic rhinitis is one of the most frequently encountered conditions in clinical practice, with allergic rhinitis being the most common subtype. The prevalence of allergic rhinitis has been steadily increasing worldwide. Unfortunately, rhinitis is often overlooked, underdiagnosed, and inadequately treated. A thorough understanding of the causes and treatment options for various types of rhinitis is essential to improve patient care and enhance the quality of life for those affected. Rhinitis has been recognized since ancient times. Seasonal allergic rhinitis, commonly known as hay fever, became more prevalent with the industrialization of Western countries in the 19th century and was widespread in Europe and North America by the late 1800s. Nonallergic Rhinitis with Eosinophilic Syndrome (NARES) was first described in 1981 by Jacobs and colleagues. Primary atrophic rhinitis has been known for centuries, with references in ancient Egyptian, Greek, and Indian medical texts. It was formally described by Bernhard Fraenkel in 1876. Rhinitis can be broadly categorized into allergic and nonallergic types. Some forms of rhinitis do not fit neatly into these categories and may exhibit features of both, referred to as mixed rhinitis. The classification and diagnosis of nonallergic rhinitis are particularly challenging due to its diverse causes and limited understanding compared to allergic rhinitis. Aeroallergens, such as dust mite fecal particles, cockroach residues, animal dander, molds, and pollens, are common triggers. These allergens are processed in the nasal tissue, leading to allergen-specific immune responses and promoting allergic airway diseases. Allergic rhinitis is typically mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE) and is associated with varying degrees of nasal inflammation. In contrast, nonallergic rhinitis encompasses a heterogeneous group of conditions with poorly understood mechanisms, requiring further research and characterization. Chronic rhinitis is a common condition seen by physicians, and identifying its underlying cause is critical for effective management. Allergic rhinitis, the most prevalent form of chronic rhinitis, is the fifth most common chronic disease in the United States. It is triggered by inhalation of indoor and outdoor aeroallergens, such as pollens, molds, and animal dander. Nonallergic rhinitis, on the other hand, is a diverse group of disorders that can be triggered by nonspecific factors, including chemical odors, cigarette smoke, spicy foods, exercise, and cold air. It is essential to distinguish rhinitis from other conditions that may mimic its symptoms, such as intranasal foreign bodies, cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea, nasal polyps, and tumors. Rhinitis is a highly prevalent condition worldwide. Allergic rhinitis affects approximately one in six Americans and is the fifth most common chronic disease in the United States. It is also the most common chronic condition in children in the U.S. The prevalence of allergic rhinitis ranges from 9% to 42%, with 30 to 60 million Americans affected annually. Of these, 10% to 30% are adults, and up to 40% are children. The prevalence of allergic rhinitis has been increasing globally, with contributing factors including rising air pollution, increased dust mite populations in poorly ventilated environments, and sedentary lifestyles. Over the past 50 years, the prevalence of allergic rhinitis has more than doubled in some countries, with over 50% of adolescents in certain regions reporting symptoms. Nonallergic rhinitis is also common, affecting an estimated 19 million people in the U.S., while mixed rhinitis is thought to affect approximately 26 million individuals. Risk factors for allergic rhinitis include a personal or family history of atopic diseases, such as asthma and atopic dermatitis. Allergic rhinitis rarely occurs in isolation. It is often associated with other atopic conditions, such as eczema, asthma, and allergic conjunctivitis. Most individuals with asthma also have rhinitis, and nearly all patients with allergic rhinitis experience allergic eye symptoms. Nonallergic rhinitis is also linked to asthma. Infectious rhinitis frequently extends into the sinuses, leading to rhinosinusitis. Children with nonallergic rhinitis are more likely to experience remission compared to those with allergic rhinitis, which tends to persist. Up to 73% of children with nonallergic rhinitis at age four achieve remission by age eight. Rhinitis significantly impacts daily life, causing missed school and workdays and imposing a substantial financial burden on society. Untreated or poorly managed chronic rhinitis is associated with reduced quality of life, sleep disturbances, impaired work performance, and various comorbidities. A thorough physical examination is essential for accurate diagnosis and management of rhinitis. This includes evaluating all organ systems potentially affected by allergies and conducting a detailed examination of the upper respiratory tract. Allergic rhinitis can be confirmed by detecting specific IgE antibodies to relevant aeroallergens through skin testing (skin-prick or intradermal tests) or serum-specific IgE testing, such as the radioallergosorbent test (RAST). Chest X-rays are not typically useful in diagnosing rhinitis unless needed to evaluate associated conditions. Similarly, CT scans are not routinely required but may be indicated in cases of complicated rhinosinusitis or suspected pathological conditions, such as atrophic rhinitis. Nasal endoscopy is a valuable diagnostic tool for identifying sinonasal pathologies and anatomical variations that may not be visible on anterior rhinoscopy. The choice of medical therapy for rhinitis depends on its cause and severity. Common treatments include antihistamines and corticosteroids. Avoiding triggers and using saline nasal irrigation can also provide significant benefits. Allergen-specific immunotherapy is recommended for selected patients with allergic rhinitis. Surgery is rarely required for rhinitis management. However, surgical intervention may be necessary to address structural or mechanical issues or to manage coexisting conditions.
